r3_s1.text: You come home late to find him at the kitchen table with your phone in his hand. The house is very quiet. “Who is this?” On the screen are messages you never meant him to read.

textIf.add: It is not the first time he has gone through it.
The name at the top of the screen is the one from the wedding. So is the word you sent back.
The thread you thought you had deleted is still there. Of course it is.
You told him about this person once. You said it was nothing, and he believed you.
There is a glass by his elbow. You don’t know how many came before it.
Once, you told him the questions bothered you. He stopped asking. Maybe this is what he did instead.
You have made excuses for him so many times. Tonight, for once, he is the one asking you to explain.

choices.label: Hand over the rest of your messages before he asks

r3_s2a.text: He is quiet. His jaw tightens, but he stays seated. The clock over the stove is suddenly very loud.

choices.recap: asked what he might be hiding too
choices.label: Ask what he might be hiding too

choices.recap: waited for him to speak first
choices.label: Wait for him to speak first

r3_s2b.text: He scrolls. “Friends don’t write this.” His voice is rising, and he is reading lines aloud now, one at a time.

r3_s2c.text: The phone hits the floor and the screen cracks. Neither of you moves. A thin line runs straight through the photo of the two of you.

choices.recap: said “Look what you made me do”
choices.label: “Look what you made me do.”

r3_s3a.text: He asks to hear it all, from the beginning. Each answer you give lands like a coin dropped into a deep well. You wait for the sound of it hitting the bottom.

choices.recap: told him only some of it
choices.label: Tell him only some of it

r3_s3b.text: He laughs once, short and flat. “Hiding? I am here every night. At this table.”

choices.recap: let the silence do the talking
choices.label: Let the silence do the talking

r3_s3c.text: He picks the phone up again and reads a line aloud in a mocking voice. Then another. The kitchen is too small for the volume.

choices.label: “Say that again and I’ll hit you.”

r3_h1.text: His chair scrapes back. Before you reach the door he is in front of it, closer than he needs to be. He keeps his voice low, which is worse than shouting. “Do that again,” he says, “and see what happens.”

textIf.add: You think of all the times he asked where you were, and how lightly he used to ask it.

choices.recap: told him he was frightening them
choices.label: “You’re frightening me.”

choices.recap: held their ground and stared back
choices.label: Hold your ground and stare back

r3_s4a.text: The silence afterwards is the longest one yet. Then: “I need to sleep in the other room tonight.”

choices.recap: asked him to stay and talk
choices.label: Ask him to stay and keep talking
Watch him pick up his coat and keys, not just a pillow

r3_s4b.text: He notices the gaps the way he notices a wobbling chair. “You’re leaving things out.”

choices.recap: said that was all there was
choices.label: Say “That’s all there is.”

r3_s4c.text: His palm comes down on the table. The cups jump. The sound fills the whole house, and you realise you have stopped breathing.

choices.recap: asked him to lower his voice
choices.label: “I need you to lower your voice.”

textIf.add: The glass by his elbow tips and rolls, and neither of you reaches for it.

r3_s4d.text: Down the hall, a small door opens an inch. One of the children is awake, and listening.

choices.recap: went to the child and closed the door gently
choices.label: Go to the child and close the door gently

choices.recap: stayed and kept their voice low
choices.label: Stay where you are and keep your voice low

r3_g1.text: He doesn’t shout. He sets the phone down on the table, very gently, like something that might break. Then he stands, pushes in his chair, and goes upstairs. A minute later you hear a zip.

choices.label: Stay at the table and give him room

choices.recap: called up the stairs to talk
choices.label: Call up the stairs: “Please, let’s talk.”

r3_g2a.text: He is folding shirts into a holdall, one at a time, with great care. “I’m not angry,” he says, without looking up. “That’s the part that frightens me.”

choices.recap: asked him to stay, for the children
choices.label: Ask him to stay, for the children

r3_g2b.text: His footsteps come down slowly. The holdall is on his shoulder. He stops at the front door, one hand on the latch. “I’ll be at my brother’s,” he says. He does not say for how long.

choices.recap: said nothing and watched the door
choices.label: Say nothing and watch the door

r3_g3a.text: He sits on the edge of the bed, bag half zipped. “I’d stay if I thought it would be different,” he says. “I think I need to be somewhere quiet, just for a while, and work out what I actually want.”

choices.recap: asked for a week and a date to talk
choices.label: Ask for one week, and a day to talk again

r3_g3b.text: He leaves that night. The first week there are short messages: “Arrived.” “Kids okay?” By the second week the replies take a day, and by the third they are only one word.

choices.recap: wrote him one long, honest message
choices.label: Write him one long, honest message

choices.recap: stopped messaging and waited for him to come back
choices.label: Stop messaging and wait for him to come back

choices.recap: told the children he was working away
choices.label: Tell the children he is “working away”

r3_g3c.text: The door closes softly behind him. There is no slam. A car starts outside, idles for a moment, and pulls away. The house settles into a silence it has never had before.

choices.label: Sit in the dark until the sound is gone

r3_g4.text: Months pass. His things stay in the wardrobe. The children stop asking when he is coming home and start asking why he doesn’t call. You are still not sure whether this is a pause or an ending.

choices.recap: wrote that the children needed him
choices.label: Write to him: “The children need to hear from you.”
Speak to a solicitor about what happens next

choices.recap: kept leaving the porch light on
choices.label: Keep leaving the porch light on

r3_end_talk.text: It goes on until three in the morning, with no shouting. Nothing is fixed, but both of you now know where things stand.

r3_end_apart.text: He takes a pillow down the hall. The door closes without a slam, which is its own kind of sound.

r3_end_standoff.text: You each retreat to your own side of the room. The phone sits face down between you, cracked.

r3_end_boil.text: He stands up too fast and the chair scrapes back. “We’re not done,” he says, and the room goes very still.

r3_end_line.text: The sentence is out before you can stop it. He does not shout back. He goes very still, and something you have never seen settles in his face. Then the kitchen fills with noise.

r3_end_threat.text: He steps aside at last, but only just enough. You have to brush past him to get out of the kitchen. Neither of you says anything. What he said is still in the room, and it follows you down the hall.

r3_end_keys.text: Neither of you looks away. Then he does, and somehow that is worse. He picks your keys up off the table, slips them into his pocket, and sits back down as if nothing has happened.

r3_end_week.text: He nods, slowly. “A week,” he says. “Saturday. Here.” He leaves with the bag, but he also leaves a date. It is not a promise, but it is more than most people get.

r3_end_message.text: You write it three times and send the third. The little word “Read” appears under it within the minute. Nothing comes back. You are not sure which is harder: being ignored, or being understood and left anyway.

r3_end_letter.text: Eleven days later an envelope arrives in his handwriting. Inside is a card for the children, and one line for you: “I’m sorry. I don’t know how to come back yet.” It is something. It is not enough.

r3_end_light.text: Every night you switch it on, and every morning you switch it off. You tell yourself it is for the children. A year from now you will realise it was a way of not deciding.

r3_end_gone.text: The solicitor asks how long he has been away, and you have to count. Then she asks whether he has contacted you, and you have to say no. The word she uses is a plain one. It is also, you realise, accurate.
